profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between two leads preparing a joint planning package for a regional emergency management consortium's upcoming Cascadia earthquake tabletop exercise. One workstream is converting a literature review on multi-agency disaster response into usable evidence products, while the other is integrating those products into facilitator materials, participant prompts, and an after-action tool. The agenda is to align on the handoff format for the case matrix, confirm what they mean by the live Cascadia deck, decide how the leadership and role-taking findings will be folded into the shared after-action template, and verify what needs to be ready for circulation before Tuesday afternoon. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on deliverables, interfaces, and timing between the research synthesis and exercise-design workstreams.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: Emergency management research, comparative case analysis, practitioner translation of disaster studies
members.background: Lena is a public policy researcher at a university-affiliated resilience center and has spent the last six months leading a review of 80 empirical studies on multi-agency disaster response. She often turns academic findings into practitioner-facing briefs and matrices, but she is less involved in the mechanics of exercise facilitation and packet assembly.
members.private_state: She wants the consortium to view the research workstream as rigorous and directly useful, and she is trying to avoid a last-minute request to strip nuance out of the synthesis after her team has already organized it for practitioner use.
hidden_assumptions: A 'case matrix' for practitioners is the detailed evidence summary matrix her team uses for handoff: roughly 15 pages, grouped by incident, with citations, study design notes, coordination themes, and highlighted takeaways that downstream teams can excerpt from.

When people mention 'the live Cascadia deck,' they are talking about the current scenario brief containing the hazard, impact, and operating-context assumptions that all downstream materials should align to.
'Ready for circulation' means polished enough to send beyond the core project team without caveats, including stable wording, cleaned citations, and no expected structural changes.
If findings are to be 'folded into the template,' the shared template owner will incorporate the wording once her team provides the inserts and annotations.
Cross-border material belongs in the common scenario framing because it shapes the operating environment agencies are expected to reason within, even if not every facilitation inject changes.

members.name: Marcus Hale
members.expertise: Interagency exercise design, facilitator tool development, regional emergency planning logistics
members.background: Marcus works for the regional emergency management consortium and is responsible for turning planning inputs into facilitator guides, participant packets, and coordination tools for county, state, healthcare, utility, and public safety partners. He routinely translates broad planning content into compact exercise-ready artifacts.
members.private_state: He needs stable inputs quickly so the exercise production schedule does not slip, and he is concerned that the research side may deliver something technically strong but too dense for facilitators to use in real time.
hidden_assumptions: A 'case matrix' is the one-page quick-reference grid used in facilitator packets, typically 8-10 exemplar incidents with short columns for trigger, coordination challenge, workaround, and discussion cue.
When people say 'the live Cascadia deck,' they mean the actively edited exercise deck his team is using to manage inject timing, player prompts, and facilitator flow decisions.
'Ready for circulation' means good enough to share with agency planning points of contact for comment, even if citations, formatting, and some wording are still provisional.

If something is to be 'folded into the template,' the contributing workstream is expected to place its content directly into the live shared document so facilitators can work from the latest version immediately.
Cross-border content only needs to appear where it affects the actions or discussion prompts of the agencies actually participating in this tabletop.

misalignment_points.topic: What the 'case matrix' looks like in the handoff
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Lena will send the case matrix for Marcus to use in the facilitator packet.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a practitioner-oriented but still comprehensive evidence summary matrix: about 15 pages, incident-organized, with citations, method notes, multiple coordination variables, and quotable takeaways that the exercise team can draw from.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a one-page facilitator quick-reference grid with a handful of exemplar incidents and very short prompts that can be dropped into the packet almost as-is.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are genuinely talking about a practitioner-facing bridge artifact between research and operations, so 'case matrix' sounds like a settled shared term rather than a point needing clarification; the difference is in degree and packaging, not in the obvious purpose of the document.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'the live Cascadia deck' refers to
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to aligning materials to 'the live Cascadia deck.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the current scenario brief deck that establishes the hazard footprint, infrastructure impacts, and cross-border operating assumptions circulated by the consortium secretariat.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of his team's actively edited exercise deck containing inject sequencing, discussion prompts, and facilitator flow for the tabletop session.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both artifacts are genuinely live, current, and called the Cascadia deck in ordinary shorthand, and because they overlap in topic and title, each person hears the phrase as naturally unambiguous within their own workflow.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the materials should be ready for circulation by Tuesday afternoon.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes this means externally polished and stable enough to send to agency representatives without expecting major edits, including cleaned citations and final framing.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes this means mature enough for internal distribution to planning contacts so they can react before the Wednesday call, even if the materials still look draft-like.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In coordination meetings, 'ready for circulation' usually functions as a routine schedule marker rather than a formal release definition, so both take the phrase as straightforward progress language and never unpack the quality threshold underneath it.

misalignment_points.topic: How findings get 'folded into the template'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the leadership and role-taking findings should be folded into the shared after-action template.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects her team to provide suggested wording and section notes, after which the exercise side, as practical owner of the template, will place those inserts into the official live structure.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects Lena's team to put the language directly into the live shared template themselves so facilitators can continue building from the updated version without an extra handoff.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrasing is passive and collaborative, which preserves the feeling of agreement about the task while hiding the difference in assumed pen-holding responsibility; in many cross-team settings, both procedures are common enough to feel like default practice.
